data.title: Vráble-Fidvár – a town from the Bronze Age (B)
data.excerpt: The tell settlement of Fidvár south of Vráble covers more than 20 hectares – more than Mycenae or Troy – and at one point housed as many as 1,000 people in houses arranged along streets. Treasure hunters came here in the 19th century, Štefan Janšák published the site in 1931, and since 2007 a Slovak–German team has been surveying it; the Sensys equipment used here was deployed for the needs of archaeology for the first time in the world.
data.metaTitle: Vráble-Fidvár – a fortified Bronze Age town (B)
data.metaDescription: Fidvár near Vráble is a tell settlement of the Early Bronze Age, larger than Mycenae or Troy, with up to 1,000 inhabitants and about 140 houses.

mediaTexts.alt: Aerial photograph of a field with cropmarks of the fortification of the Fidvár site

children.text: The site of Fidvár, or Zemný hrad (Foldvár – earthwork fort, Hung.), lies south of Vráble. It has always attracted attention. The first information about the site dates from the 19th century. At that time it was visited by many treasure hunters – the so-called first archaeologists. Among them was the royal postmaster of Vráble, Jozef Néčei.

At Fidvár he discovered interesting objects of the Maďarovce culture, Roman oil lamps, objects of the Stone Age, various axe-hammers, various bronze ornaments and even skates made of bone! His finds later ended up in Levice, where after Néčei’s death the Tekov Museum was established. To this day the museum holds hundreds of archaeological objects from the Fidvár site near Vráble.

For a long time the site “lay” untouched. At the beginning and in the middle of the 20th century, in the time of the two world wars, the site lay untouched. After the Second World War it attracted, from time to time, more and more treasure hunters.

blocks.alt: Vráble-Fidvár – a town from the Bronze Age (B)

children.text: In 1931 the “Sborník Muzeálnej Slovenskej spoločnosti” (Proceedings of the Slovak Museum Society) in Turčiansky Svätý Martin published an article entitled “Hradište pri Vrábľoch a skupina sídlisk pri Žitva-Ďarmotách” (The hillfort near Vráble and the group of settlements near Žitva-Ďarmoty). The article was written by the archaeologist Štefan Janšák, the first specialist to carry out an investigation here. In the article he writes about the peninsulas that occurred at the Fidvár site, where a fortified settlement was said to have stood in prehistory and a castle in the Middle Ages. At Fidvár, Janšák saw black circles in the clayey-sandy topsoil. These were the remains of large hearths or occupation pits. In the article Janšák wrote: “The centre of occupation of this region is the artificially built hillfort near Vráble. That life was concentrated here is indicated not only by the numerous remains of old cultures, but chiefly by the defences in the form of ditches. The principle of construction lay in the fact that a piece of the terrace, with a fairly steep and high natural step towards the water, was separated by a ditch from the rest of the bank. The builders of the hillfort dug a ditch 6 metres deep at its lowest point and 3 metres at its highest point. /…/ To the south and to the north of this artificial mound there is a great quantity of sherds, proof that the whole surrounding area was occupied.” Janšák mentions that the hill had been dug into and that sand and clay were taken from it for building. This hillfort was already known to Romer in the work “Résultats généraux du mouvement archéologique en Hongrie”, published in Budapest in 1878. Janšák noted that on the Fidvár knoll there was an incredibly large quantity of sherds, which made it look like some sort of stony hill. “Not only the artificially built hillfort itself, but the whole surface of the peninsula between the little river Žitava and the brook coming from the east, is strewn with a strikingly large quantity of sherds. Their fragments lie literally one beside another, so that they even hinder the cultivation of the field. They make it stony and less fertile.”

children.text: The site did not experience a real archaeological excavation until the 1960s, when it was visited by scholars from the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra. At that time the site was investigated by the archaeologist Točík. They dug a trench, which did not reveal much, however. They found many sherds and traces of dwellings, but nothing ground-breaking.

The Fidvár site is in fact a prehistoric settlement of the so-called tell type, that is, a settlement mound. It is a multi-layered settlement, which came into being because people lived in one place for several millennia, modifying, levelling and raising the terrain and so on. In this way an occupation layer even several metres thick was formed (at Vráble specifically it is over 2 m thick, and the oldest layers belong to the Eneolithic and the youngest to the Early Bronze Age. In such a tell archaeologists can then “leaf through” the layers as through a calendar, because the oldest layers lie right at the bottom and the youngest at the top. The significance of this site at Vráble also lies in the fact that it is the northernmost site of tell type within the Carpathian Basin!

blocks.alt: Vráble-Fidvár – a town from the Bronze Age (B)

children.text: North of the Fidvár site, closer to the town of Vráble, an anti-Ottoman Renaissance fortress with four bastions stood from 1624 to 1698. It took its name from the historical name of the town – Werebel. To this day people confuse the name Fidvár – Zemný hrad with the name of the castle of Vráble. Fidvár was a prehistoric fortress – an enormous settlement, a village – whereas the Renaissance fortress stood for barely a century closer to Vráble. The fact that the Renaissance fortress stood further away from the prehistoric fortress of Fidvár proved to be an excellent solution on the part of our forebears. For the prehistoric settlement remained practically untouched for a full 4,000 years!

In 2007 the well-known Slovak archaeologist and specialist in the Bronze Age of Central and Eastern Europe, Prof. PhDr. Jozef Bátora, DrSc., visited the Fidvár site near Vráble together with German archaeologists from Frankfurt am Main in order to begin uncovering the mysteries of this site step by step. In the first year of the project the archaeologists carried out a surface collection and surveyed the whole area by geomagnetic measurement. During this survey the archaeologists used the most modern technologies, such as are commonly employed in Germany, England or Egypt. Another world first was that they surveyed the largest area to date (23 ha) by geomagnetic measurement.

blocks.alt: Vráble-Fidvár – a town from the Bronze Age (B)

children.text: During three weeks of intensive excavation the archaeologists concluded that the Fidvár site holds the largest settlement agglomeration of the Early Bronze Age not only in Slovakia but in the whole of Europe. It covers an area of more than 20 hectares and is therefore larger than Mycenae or Troy in Asia Minor! The Vráble settlement – the fortress of Fidvár – is roughly 3,000 years old. Similar settlements have been found in Europe which at a given moment were inhabited by about 100 people. At Fidvár, however, there was an unprecedented concentration of population. At one point as many as 1,000 inhabitants lived there. The settlement consisted of several ditches. It was a circular settlement with a diameter of as much as 220 m. Around the settlement, in turn, stood a number of further houses. The upper social stratum lived in the centre, the common people on the periphery. There were several craft workshops in the settlement. Within the fortified area stood a number of houses arranged into streets. It was in fact a settlement of urban character, resembling a town.

children.text: In 2008 the excavation at Fidvár continued once again, in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology in Nitra, the RGK DAI in Frankfurt am Main and the University of Würzburg. As regards the results of the excavation at Fidvár, the archaeologists once again gained interesting insights.

The foremost aim of the excavation in that year was to verify the results of the geomagnetic measurements, by which in the previous year the archaeologists had identified, besides two ditches, the ground plans of about 140 rectangular features, probably houses. The archaeologists carried out this verification by digging conventional trenches at 7 places – where the ground plans of these houses showed up most clearly.

The trench confirmed that houses really do lie in the ground, but that their lower parts were not of stone but of burnt clay – daub. The archaeologists were surprised by the well-preserved ground plans and the large dimensions. The houses were in fact 8–10 m long and 4 m wide. In one case Prof. Bátora believes that they uncovered a destroyed house with an upper storey.

blocks.alt: Vráble-Fidvár – a town from the Bronze Age (B)

children.text: A significant success of this year’s excavation was the cemetery discovered by test trenching, which belongs to the Únětice phase of the occupation of Fidvár. It is an inhumation cemetery in which the dead were buried west–east and east–west. A further aim of this year’s excavation was to investigate the western edge of the settlement, which already lies in a small wood, below which the river Žitava once flowed close by. In the Middle Ages there was a large lake there. The test trenching showed that in this part of the settlement part of the defences is missing to the archaeologists. This was caused by the river Žitava, which washed the fortification away during floods.

Besides the excavation work, the archaeologists from Slovakia and Germany continued with the geomagnetic measurements, which showed that the area of the settlement is considerably larger than they had assumed in 2007. It therefore covers more than 20 hectares!

At the end of this year’s excavation (in the month of September), exceptionally powerful equipment was deployed thanks to the director of the German Archaeological Institute in Frankfurt am Main, Prof. Dr F. Lüth, who visited the Fidvár site in person. The measurements at the Fidvár site were carried out by the German company Sensys. The instrument was far more accurate than any the archaeologists had had until then. Thanks to this survey they learned that the houses mentioned had a hearth in the middle and also traces of post holes. Thanks to this survey the archaeologists also managed to discover three further cemeteries where the inhabitants of Fidvár were buried. The discovery of the cemeteries increased still further the already great historical value of Fidvár.

blocks.alt: Vráble-Fidvár – a town from the Bronze Age (B)

children.text: Finally, it is important to note that Sensys is in fact a company serving military purposes, the locating of munitions, and that it had until then been deployed at battle sites in, for example, Kosovo and the former Yugoslavia. It was precisely at Vráble that it was deployed for the needs of archaeology for the first time in the world!!!

This year’s excavation brought a further advance in uncovering the mysterious site of Fidvár near Vráble, one that will help to clarify the life of people in the Bronze Age not only in Slovakia but in the whole of Europe.
